chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Sulaym al-Farra, from one who narrated it to him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
When you supplicate, think that your need is at the door (imminent).

key_terms.بِالْبَابِ: at the door — a vivid metaphor for imminence; the fulfilment is right there, waiting to enter
key_terms.حَاجَة: need/want — refers to what one is asking of God in supplication
key_terms.دَعَوْتَ: supplicated/prayed — from the root da'a (to call, to invoke), referring specifically to petitionary prayer
key_terms.فَظُنَّ: then think/believe — from dhann, but here used in the positive sense of confident expectation, not mere conjecture

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about having certainty when making du'a?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) instructs believers to approach supplication with complete conviction that God will answer their prayer imminently. The Arabic idiom 'your need is at the door' vividly conveys the certainty and immediacy with which the supplicant should expect God's response. This teaching addresses the importance of yaqin (certainty) as a prerequisite for sincere du'a, as doubt or hesitancy weakens the spiritual quality of the supplication.
